faqs: What is PPC management?

PPC management is the ongoing setup, monitoring and optimisation of pay-per-click ad campaigns — keyword and audience targeting, ad copy, bids, budgets, tracking and landing pages — to get the most leads or sales for your ad spend.
How much should I spend on Google Ads?

It depends on your industry’s cost per click and how many leads you need. We’ll estimate a realistic starting budget from keyword data during your free consultation, start controlled, and scale once campaigns are profitable.
Is the management fee separate from ad spend?
Yes. Ad spend is paid directly to the ad platform from your own account. Our monthly management fee covers strategy, setup, optimisation and reporting.
How quickly will I see results from PPC?
Ads can start generating clicks and enquiries within days of launch. Campaigns usually become significantly more efficient over the first 4–8 weeks as we gather data and optimise.
Should I do PPC or SEO?

PPC brings immediate traffic while you pay for it; SEO builds traffic that compounds over time. Many clients run both: PPC for instant leads and keyword data, SEO to lower long-term acquisition costs.

process: We study your industry, competitors, and existing backlink profile to build a strategy tailored to your goals.
Our outreach specialists connect with reputable websites and blogs relevant to your niche.
We craft valuable, SEO-optimised content that naturally includes your backlinks.
Backlinks are placed contextually on authority sites with high domain ratings for maximum impact.
faqs: How much does link building cost?

Our link building packages start at $3.49 for 2 dofollow backlinks on a DA 10+ site and go up to $64.49 for 10 editorial backlinks from DA 50+ websites with 1,000-word content. Every package is a one-off price with a placement report.
Are your backlinks dofollow?
Yes. Our packages deliver dofollow backlinks placed contextually within relevant content. Profile backlinks in the Standard Boost plan diversify your link profile alongside guest posts.
Is link building safe for my website?

Yes, when it is done the way we do it: manual outreach to real, niche-relevant websites with genuine content. We never use private blog networks or automated link spam, which are what trigger Google penalties.
How long until backlinks improve my rankings?
Links are usually indexed within a few weeks of going live. Ranking improvements typically follow over 4–12 weeks, depending on your competition and how relevant the linking sites are to your niche.
What is the difference between DA and DR?

Domain Authority (DA, by Moz) and Domain Rating (DR, by Ahrefs) are third-party scores from 0–100 estimating a site’s backlink strength. Google doesn’t use either directly, so we also check real traffic, relevance and link profile quality before placing your links.
Will I get a report of my links?
Yes. Every order includes a placement report with the live URL of each link; higher plans add metrics such as authority and traffic for each linking site.

Standard SEO at $499/month adds a technical audit, 20 backlinks and a content strategy. Larger or international projects are quoted on our Custom SEO plan.
How long does SEO take to work?

Most websites see first ranking movements within 4–8 weeks of on-page and technical fixes going live. Meaningful traffic and lead growth typically builds over 3–6 months, depending on your competition, your site’s history and how many keywords you target.
What is included in an SEO package?

Every plan includes keyword research, on-page optimisation of your key pages, meta title and description optimisation and a monthly performance report. Higher plans add technical SEO audits and fixes, link building, local SEO, content strategy and written articles.
Do you offer local SEO for UK businesses?

Yes. Local SEO is included from our Premium plan and available on request. We optimise your Google Business Profile, build consistent local citations and create location-relevant content so you show up in the map pack and “near me” searches.
Do you guarantee first-page rankings?

No honest agency can guarantee rankings — Google controls the algorithm. What we guarantee is the work: every deliverable in your package, done to best practice, with transparent monthly reporting so you can see exactly what was done and what moved.
Is your SEO white-hat and Google-safe?
Yes. We follow Google’s Search Essentials and spam policies: no private blog networks, no link schemes, no keyword stuffing. That protects your site from penalties and builds rankings that last.

Consistency matters more than volume. For most small businesses, 3–5 quality posts a week on one or two core platforms outperforms daily low-effort posting everywhere.

posts.title: How Much Does SEO Cost in 2026? Prices, Packages & What You Actually Get
posts.excerpt: SEO typically costs $300–$2,000+ a month for small and mid-sized businesses. Here’s what drives the price, what each budget really buys, and how to spot a package worth paying for.
posts.rm_title: How Much Does SEO Cost in 2026? Prices & Packages Explained
posts.rm_desc: SEO typically costs $300–$2,000+ per month. See what drives SEO pricing, what each budget buys, and how to choose an SEO package that pays for itself.
posts.image_title: How Much Does SEO Cost in 2026?
posts.image_sub: Prices, packages and what you actually get
posts.image_alt: Illustration of an SEO dashboard showing organic traffic growth, for a guide to SEO pricing
takeaways: Most small and mid-sized businesses spend $300–$2,000 per month on SEO; enterprise and large e-commerce projects cost more.
Price is driven by competition, the number of keywords and pages, technical debt and how much content and link building you need.
Cheap SEO usually means automated links or no real work — both can cost you more than they save.
A good package lists every deliverable, reports monthly and is honest that results build over 3–6 months.
faqs: How much should a small business spend on SEO?

Most small businesses get meaningful results from $300–$600 per month when they focus on a tight set of local or niche keywords. Competitive national markets usually need $1,000+ per month to cover content and link building.
Is SEO a one-off cost or monthly?
Both exist. A one-off audit or setup fixes foundations, but rankings are competitive and Google updates constantly, so most businesses pay monthly for ongoing optimisation, content and links.
Why are some SEO packages so cheap?
Very cheap packages often rely on automated directory links or do little actual work. Ask exactly what will be delivered each month and how it will be reported. If the answer is vague, walk away.
How long before SEO pays for itself?
Expect first movements in 4–8 weeks and stronger results at 3–6 months. In competitive markets it can take longer, but unlike ads, the traffic keeps coming without paying per click.
posts.content:
Short answer: most small and mid-sized businesses pay between $300 and $2,000 per month for professional SEO in 2026. Local businesses targeting a handful of keywords sit at the lower end; e-commerce stores and competitive national brands sit at the top or above. What matters more than the number is what you get for it — and that’s where most buyers get burned.

We price and deliver SEO every day, so this guide breaks down exactly what drives the cost, what each budget level should realistically include, and the red flags that tell you a “cheap” package will end up expensive.

Typical SEO pricing in 2026

SEO is sold in three main ways. Monthly retainers are the most common because rankings are earned and defended over time, not fixed once.

Pricing modelTypical rangeBest for
Monthly retainer$300–$2,000+ / monthOngoing growth: content, links, technical upkeep and reporting
One-off SEO audit$150–$1,500Finding and prioritising technical and on-page problems
Project-based$500–$5,000+Site migrations, relaunches, large content builds
Hourly consulting$75–$200 / hourIn-house teams that need expert guidance

What actually drives the cost of SEO?

1. How competitive your market is

Ranking a plumber in one town is a different job from ranking a national insurance comparison site. The more established competitors you face, the more content and authority (backlinks) you need to overtake them — and that is where most of the budget goes.

2. The number of keywords and pages

Every keyword you target needs a page that genuinely deserves to rank: researched, written, optimised and internally linked. Five keywords and five pages is a very different workload from fifty.

3. Technical debt

Slow pages, broken links, duplicate content, indexing problems and poor mobile experience all hold rankings back. Sites with years of accumulated issues need more work up front. Google’s own Core Web Vitals guidance is a good benchmark for what “fast enough” means.

4. Content and link building

Content and backlinks are the two biggest variable costs. A package that includes written articles and real, manually outreached links will cost more than one that only tweaks meta tags — and it will also be the one that moves rankings.

5. Local vs national vs international

Local SEO focuses on your Google Business Profile, reviews, citations and location pages. National and international SEO needs more content, more authority and often multiple languages or regions.

What each SEO budget should include

Here’s a realistic view of what you should expect at each level. It mirrors how we structure our own monthly SEO packages.

  • $300–$500 / month: keyword research for 5–20 keywords, on-page optimisation of your key pages, technical fixes, analytics setup and a monthly report. Our Basic SEO ($299) and Standard SEO ($499) plans sit here — Standard adds a technical audit, 20 backlinks and a content strategy.
  • $1,000–$1,500 / month: everything above for 30–50 keywords, plus regular articles, advanced local SEO, site speed work and an ongoing link building campaign — see Premium SEO and Enterprise SEO.
  • $1,500–$2,500+ / month: e-commerce or highly competitive projects: product and category optimisation at scale, 100+ backlinks, weekly reporting with revenue tracking. Our E-commerce SEO plan is built for this.

Not sure which level you need? Tell us your website and goals and we’ll recommend the smallest package that can realistically move the needle. Get a free recommendation →

Red flags: when cheap SEO gets expensive

  • Guaranteed #1 rankings. Nobody controls Google’s algorithm. Guarantees usually mean tricks that don’t last.
  • “1,000 backlinks for $50”. Bulk automated links break Google’s spam policies and can trigger penalties that take months to recover from.
  • No list of deliverables. If you can’t see exactly what will be done each month, you can’t hold anyone accountable.
  • Reports full of vanity metrics. Impressions and “visibility scores” mean little. You want rankings for keywords that convert, organic traffic and enquiries or sales.
  • Long lock-in contracts with no exit. Good agencies keep clients through results, not contracts.

How to judge whether SEO is worth it

Do the simple maths. Estimate how many extra visitors the target keywords could bring, multiply by your conversion rate and average customer value, and compare it with the monthly fee. A $499 package only needs to win a couple of clients a month for many service businesses to be profitable — and unlike paid ads, the traffic doesn’t stop when you stop paying.

Then give it time. Most sites see first movements within 4–8 weeks of technical and on-page fixes, with stronger gains at 3–6 months. If you need leads tomorrow, pair SEO with PPC while organic rankings build.

The bottom line

SEO costs what it costs because the work — research, content, technical fixes and genuine links — takes skilled time. Pay for a clear list of deliverables, honest timelines and reporting tied to business results. If you’d like to see exactly what that looks like, compare our SEO packages side by side.

posts.excerpt: A practical, step-by-step local SEO checklist covering your Google Business Profile, reviews, citations, location pages and on-site signals — the exact things that move map pack rankings.

posts.image_alt: Illustration of local search rankings for a local SEO checklist
takeaways: Google ranks local results on relevance, distance and prominence — you can influence relevance and prominence.
Your Google Business Profile is the single most important local ranking asset; complete every field and keep it active.
Consistent name, address and phone (NAP) across the web builds trust with Google.

faqs: How long does local SEO take?
Profile and citation fixes can show results in a few weeks. Competitive cities usually take 3–6 months of consistent reviews, content and links to reach the top three.
Do I need a physical address for local SEO?
You need a real address to verify a Google Business Profile, but service-area businesses can hide it and list the areas they serve instead.
Do reviews affect local rankings?
Yes. The number, recency and quality of reviews — and your replies — are part of Google’s prominence signals, and they strongly influence clicks and calls.
posts.content:
Local SEO is how your business shows up when people nearby search for what you sell — the map pack, “near me” searches and Google Maps. Google says local results are ranked on three things: relevance, distance and prominence. You can’t move your shop, but you can absolutely improve relevance and prominence. This checklist is the exact order we work through for clients.

Google Business Profile (steps 1–7)

  1. Claim and verify your profile using the exact business name you trade under — no keyword stuffing.
  2. Choose the most accurate primary category. This is one of the strongest relevance signals. Add secondary categories only if they genuinely apply.
  3. Complete every field: hours, phone, website, services, products, attributes and a keyword-natural description.
  4. Add real photos of your premises, team and work. Update them regularly.
  5. Set your service areas accurately if you travel to customers.
  6. Post updates weekly or fortnightly — offers, projects, news. Activity signals a live business.
  7. Use the Q&A section to answer the questions customers actually ask before buying.

Reviews and reputation (steps 8–11)

  1. Ask every happy customer for a review with a direct link. Timing matters: ask right after a successful job.
  2. Reply to every review, good and bad, professionally and quickly.
  3. Never buy or gate reviews. Fake reviews break Google’s rules and, in the UK, consumer law.
  4. Build reviews on other trusted platforms relevant to your industry (Trustpilot, Yelp, industry directories).

Citations and NAP consistency (steps 12–14)

  1. Standardise your name, address and phone (NAP) and use the exact same format everywhere.
  2. List your business on major directories and data aggregators for your country.
  3. Fix duplicates and outdated listings — old addresses and phone numbers confuse Google and customers.

Citations and profile links are part of our link building packages — the Standard Boost plan combines guest posts with profile links for a natural local footprint.

On-site local signals (steps 15–18)

  1. Create a dedicated page for each service and location you genuinely serve, with unique content — not copy-pasted city names.
  2. Add LocalBusiness schema with your NAP, hours and geo-coordinates.
  3. Embed your address and a map on your contact page and show NAP in the footer.
  4. Make it fast and mobile-friendly. Most local searches happen on phones.

Local authority (steps 19–20)

  1. Earn local links: sponsorships, local news, suppliers, chambers of commerce and community partnerships.
  2. Publish locally useful content — guides, case studies and FAQs that local customers search for.

How to track local SEO progress

Track map pack rankings for your main keywords from several points in your area, plus Google Business Profile calls, direction requests and website clicks. Those are the numbers that turn into revenue.

Want this done for you? Advanced local SEO is built into our Premium SEO package, and available on any plan. See SEO packages →

Summary

Local SEO rewards businesses that look complete, active and trusted. Nail your Google Business Profile, earn genuine reviews, keep your NAP consistent and back it up with real location pages and local links. Work through this checklist in order and you’ll be ahead of most competitors in your area.

posts.title: Technical SEO Audit Checklist: 25 Checks That Actually Move Rankings
posts.excerpt: A no-fluff technical SEO audit checklist: crawling, indexing, site speed, Core Web Vitals, mobile, structured data and internal links — with what to fix first.
posts.rm_title: Technical SEO Audit Checklist: 25 Checks That Move Rankings
posts.rm_desc: A practical technical SEO audit checklist: crawlability, indexing, Core Web Vitals, mobile, structured data and internal linking — and what to fix first.
posts.image_alt: Illustration of a website performance dashboard for a technical SEO audit checklist
takeaways: If Google can’t crawl and index a page, nothing else matters — start every audit there.
Core Web Vitals and mobile usability affect both rankings and conversions.
Duplicate content, redirect chains and orphan pages quietly waste crawl budget and authority.
Prioritise fixes by impact: indexing blockers first, then speed, then structure and enhancements.
faqs: How often should I run a technical SEO audit?
Run a full audit at least twice a year and after any redesign, migration or platform change. Monitor Search Console weekly for new errors.
What tools do I need for a technical SEO audit?
Google Search Console and PageSpeed Insights are free and essential. A crawler such as Screaming Frog, plus Ahrefs or Semrush, makes larger audits much faster.
Can technical SEO alone improve rankings?
Fixing blockers can produce quick wins, especially for sites with indexing or speed problems. Long-term growth still needs strong content and backlinks.
posts.content:
A technical SEO audit checks whether search engines can find, crawl, render and index your website efficiently — and whether real users get a fast, stable experience. It’s the foundation every other SEO effort sits on. Here are the 25 checks we run on every client site, grouped by priority.

Priority 1: crawling and indexing

  1. Robots.txt isn’t blocking important pages, CSS or JavaScript.
  2. XML sitemap exists, is submitted in Search Console and only lists indexable, 200-status URLs.
  3. Index coverage: review Search Console’s Pages report for “Crawled – currently not indexed” and “Excluded” surprises.
  4. Noindex tags are only on pages that should be hidden (cart, checkout, thank-you pages).
  5. Canonical tags point to the preferred version of each page.
  6. One version of the site: HTTP, HTTPS, www and non-www all 301 to a single canonical origin.
  7. Status codes: no important pages returning 404 or 5xx errors.

Priority 2: speed and Core Web Vitals

  1. Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds on mobile.
  2. Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds.
  3. Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1 — set width and height on images and embeds.
  4. Images compressed, in modern formats (WebP/AVIF) and lazy-loaded below the fold.
  5. Render-blocking CSS and JavaScript minimised; unused plugins removed.
  6. Caching and a CDN enabled; server response time (TTFB) under 600ms.

Google’s Web Vitals documentation explains each metric in detail.

Priority 3: site structure and internal links

  1. Every important page is reachable within three clicks of the homepage.
  2. No orphan pages — every page has at least one internal link pointing to it.
  3. Redirect chains and loops are flattened to a single 301.
  4. Broken internal links are fixed at the source, not just redirected.
  5. Clean, descriptive URLs without parameters for content pages.
  6. Breadcrumbs on deeper pages for users and search engines.

Priority 4: on-page technical elements

  1. Unique title tags and meta descriptions on every indexable page.
  2. One H1 per page with a logical H2–H3 hierarchy.
  3. Duplicate and thin content consolidated or improved.
  4. Image alt text that describes the image.

Priority 5: enhancements

  1. Structured data (Organization, Product, Article, FAQ, Breadcrumb) validates in Google’s Rich Results Test.
  2. Mobile usability: readable text, tappable buttons, no horizontal scrolling.

How to prioritise what you find

Audits often surface hundreds of issues. Fix in this order: anything stopping important pages being indexed, then speed problems on your highest-traffic templates, then structural and internal linking issues, and finally enhancements like schema. One template fix can resolve thousands of URLs at once — always look for the root cause.

Final thoughts

Technical SEO isn’t glamorous, but it multiplies the return on everything else you do. A fast, crawlable, well-structured site lets your content and backlinks do their job. faqs: Is link building still important in 2026?
Yes. Links remain a core way search engines measure authority. What has changed is that low-quality, manipulative links are ignored or penalised, so quality matters more than ever.
How many backlinks do I need?
There’s no fixed number. Compare the referring domains of the pages ranking above you for your target keyword; that’s your realistic benchmark.
What is a dofollow link?
A normal link that passes ranking signals. Links marked rel="nofollow", "sponsored" or "ugc" are hints to Google not to pass full credit.
Can bad backlinks hurt my site?
Google mostly ignores spammy links, but large-scale manipulative link building can lead to a manual action. If you have a history of paid spam links, an audit is worthwhile.
posts.content:
Link building is the process of getting other websites to link to yours. Search engines treat each relevant link as a vote of confidence: the more trusted sites that reference your content, the more authoritative your site appears. In 2026, backlinks remain one of the strongest ranking factors — but how you get them matters more than ever.

Why backlinks matter for SEO

Google’s original breakthrough was using links to judge which pages deserve to rank. That principle still holds. Links help search engines discover your pages, understand what they’re about from the surrounding context and anchor text, and decide how much to trust them. In competitive niches, content alone rarely wins without authority behind it.

What makes a good backlink?

FactorGood linkBad link
RelevanceSite in your industry or a closely related topicUnrelated site (casino link on a bakery blog)
AuthorityEstablished site with real organic trafficNew or expired domain with no visitors
PlacementContextual link inside useful contentFooter, sidebar or a page full of links
Anchor textNatural, varied wordingExact-match keyword stuffing
SourceEarned via outreach, PR or great contentBought in bulk from a link network

White-hat link building methods that work

Guest posting on relevant sites

Writing genuinely useful articles for respected blogs and publications in your niche, with a natural link back to a relevant page on your site.

Broken link building

Finding broken links on relevant sites and suggesting your content as a replacement. It helps the site owner and earns you a contextual link.

Digital PR and linkable assets

Original data, tools, guides and expert commentary that journalists and bloggers want to cite.

Business citations and profiles

Accurate listings on trusted directories and industry platforms. They’re foundational rather than powerful, but they build a natural profile and support local SEO.

Competitor link analysis

Studying which sites link to your competitors reveals proven opportunities for your own outreach.

Link building tactics to avoid

  • Buying hundreds of links from “packages” that never name the sites.
  • Private blog networks (PBNs) and link farms.
  • Automated comment, forum or profile spam.
  • Large-scale link exchanges and exact-match anchor text everywhere.

Google’s spam policies specifically call out link schemes. They’re not worth the risk.

How we approach link building

Conclusion

Link building works when it mirrors how the web naturally works: relevant sites referencing genuinely useful pages. Focus on relevance, real traffic and natural placements, avoid shortcuts, and your authority — and rankings — will compound over time.

posts.title: SEO Content Writing: How to Write Content That Ranks (and Gets Cited by AI)
posts.excerpt: A practical framework for SEO content writing in 2026: search intent, structure, E-E-A-T, internal links and the formatting that helps both Google and AI assistants quote you.

posts.rm_desc: SEO content writing that ranks and gets cited by AI: match search intent, structure for skimmers, show E-E-A-T and link internally.
posts.image_sub: And gets cited by AI assistants
posts.image_alt: Illustration of a blog post draft with SEO keyword tags for an SEO content writing guide
takeaways: Start with search intent: give searchers the format and answer they expect.
Answer the main question in the first two sentences, then go deeper.
Show real experience and expertise (E-E-A-T) — examples, data, named authors.
Clear headings, lists, tables and FAQs help readers, Google and AI assistants alike.
faqs: How long should an SEO article be?
As long as it needs to be to fully answer the query — no longer. Check the top-ranking pages for a guide, then aim to be more useful, not just longer.
Should I use AI to write SEO content?
AI can help with research and outlines, but publishing unedited AI text rarely ranks well or builds trust. Human expertise, editing and original insight are what make content stand out.
How many keywords should one page target?
One primary topic per page, supported by closely related phrases and questions. Separate intents deserve separate pages.
posts.content:
SEO content writing is creating content that answers what people search for, in a way search engines can understand and readers trust enough to act on. In 2026 it has a second job: being clear and well-structured enough that AI assistants like Google’s AI Overviews and ChatGPT quote it. The good news is that the same principles win on both fronts.

1. Start with search intent

Before writing a word, search your target keyword and study the results. Are they guides, lists, product pages or local results? That’s Google telling you what searchers want. Match the format, then beat it on depth, clarity and usefulness.

  • Informational: “what is link building” → a clear explainer.
  • Commercial: “best SEO packages” → comparisons and pricing.
  • Transactional: “buy SEO audit” → a service or product page.
  • Local: “web designer near me” → location pages and a strong Google Business Profile.

2. Answer first, then expand

Put the direct answer in the first two sentences — a definition, a number or a recommendation. Readers stay, Google can lift it for a featured snippet, and AI tools can quote it accurately. Then use the rest of the page to explain, prove and add nuance.

3. Structure for skimmers (and machines)

  • Descriptive H2s that read like the questions people ask.
  • Short paragraphs, bullet lists and numbered steps.
  • Tables for comparisons and prices.
  • An FAQ section for related questions.
  • A “key takeaways” box near the top of long guides.

4. Show E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authority, trust

Google’s guidance on helpful, people-first content rewards content written by people who know the subject. Add first-hand examples, original screenshots or data, a named author with a real bio, and accurate sources. Keep facts up to date and show when the page was last reviewed.

5. Optimise without stuffing

  • Use the primary keyword naturally in the title, H1, first paragraph and URL.
  • Cover the related subtopics and entities competitors mention — that’s semantic relevance.
  • Write a compelling meta title (≈60 characters) and description (≈155 characters).
  • Add descriptive image alt text.

6. Link internally with intent

Every new article should link to the service or product it supports, and older related posts should link back to it. Internal links spread authority and guide readers toward conversion — for example, this guide links to our SEO content writing service.

7. Update content on a schedule

Rankings decay as information ages and competitors improve. Review your top pages every 6–12 months: refresh facts, add new questions and tighten the introduction.

A simple SEO content checklist

  1. Intent and format match the current top results.
  2. The main question is answered in the first two sentences.
  3. Headings cover the full topic and related questions.
  4. Real experience, examples or data are included.
  5. The author is named, with relevant expertise.
  6. Meta title, description and alt text are written.
  7. It links to and from relevant pages.

Conclusion

Great SEO content is simply great content that’s easy to find and easy to understand. Write for the person searching, structure it so they — and the machines — can find answers fast, and keep it current.

faqs: Which is cheaper, Google Ads or Facebook Ads?
Facebook often has lower cost per click, but Google search clicks usually convert at a higher rate because of intent. Compare cost per lead or cost per sale instead.
How much budget do I need to start PPC?
Enough to gather meaningful data — often a few hundred dollars per month per platform for small local campaigns, more in competitive industries. Start controlled and scale what converts.
Can I run both platforms together?
Yes, and it’s often the most effective approach: search captures demand, social builds awareness and retargets visitors who didn’t convert.
posts.content:
The short version: Google Ads is usually better when people are already searching for what you sell, while Facebook and Instagram ads are better for creating demand and reaching people before they search. The right choice depends on your product, your buyers and your budget — and for many businesses the answer is both.

Google Ads vs Facebook Ads at a glance

Google AdsFacebook & Instagram Ads
How you reach peopleKeywords people search forInterests, behaviours, lookalikes, retargeting
User intentHigh — actively lookingLower — browsing, discovering
Best forServices, urgent needs, high-intent productsVisual products, new offers, brand awareness
CreativeText ads, Shopping, video, Performance MaxImages, video, carousels, Reels
Typical CPCHigherLower
Conversion rateUsually higherUsually lower, improves with retargeting

When Google Ads wins

  • Your customers search with clear intent (“emergency electrician”, “accountant near me”).
  • You sell a product people already know they want and compare on price.
  • You need leads quickly and can measure enquiries or sales accurately.

When Facebook and Instagram ads win

  • Your product is visual, new or impulse-friendly.
  • You can define your audience by interests, life events or demographics.
  • You want to build awareness, an audience or an email list.
  • You need to retarget website visitors who didn’t buy.

Measure the right metric

Cost per click is misleading. A $6 Google click that converts at 8% can be far cheaper per customer than a $1 social click that converts at 0.5%. Set up conversion tracking properly — GA4 plus the Google tag and Meta Pixel — and compare cost per lead, cost per sale and return on ad spend.

The best of both: a combined funnel

  1. Search ads capture people ready to buy now.
  2. Social ads introduce your brand to new audiences.
  3. Retargeting on both platforms brings back visitors who didn’t convert.
  4. Landing pages matched to each ad lift conversion rates across the board.

Common PPC mistakes to avoid

  • Running ads before conversion tracking works.
  • Broad keywords with no negative keyword list.
  • Sending all traffic to the homepage instead of a focused landing page.
  • Judging campaigns after a few days instead of a few weeks of data.

Conclusion

If people already search for what you sell, start with Google Ads. If you need to create demand or sell visually, start with Meta. Once one channel is profitable, add the other for reach and retargeting. Our PPC management team can help you decide and run both.

faqs: Which social media platform is best for a small business?
It depends on your audience: Instagram and TikTok for consumer and visual brands, Facebook for local communities and older audiences, LinkedIn for B2B.
How often should a small business post?
Three to five quality posts a week on your main platform is a sustainable target for most small businesses.
Should I pay for social media ads?
Organic content builds trust; paid ads speed up reach and retargeting. Most growing businesses benefit from a small, well-targeted ad budget once their organic content is consistent.
posts.content:
A social media marketing strategy is a plan for which platforms you’ll use, what you’ll post, how often, and how that activity turns into customers. Most small businesses don’t fail on social because of a lack of ideas — they fail because there’s no plan, so posting becomes random and stops. Here’s a realistic 90-day plan you can follow.

Days 1–14: foundations

Set one clear goal

Pick a goal you can measure: website enquiries, bookings, online sales or email sign-ups. Followers are a means, not the goal.

Choose your platforms

  • Instagram: visual products, lifestyle, local services, Reels.
  • Facebook: local communities, events, groups and older audiences.
  • LinkedIn: B2B services, professional expertise and hiring.
  • TikTok: short-form video and younger audiences.

Start with one or two. You can expand once the first is working.

Optimise your profiles

Consistent name and branding, a clear bio that says what you do and who for, a link to a relevant landing page, and contact details.

Days 15–30: content pillars and calendar

Content pillars are the 3–4 themes you’ll post about repeatedly. For example, a café might use behind the scenes, menu highlights, customer stories and local community. A B2B agency might use tips, case studies, team and industry news.

FridayCustomer proofTestimonial or result
Weekend (optional)Offer or communitySingle image or story

Days 31–60: publish, engage, learn

  • Post consistently on your calendar — batch-create content weekly.
  • Reply to comments and messages within a day; engagement is part of the algorithm and of customer service.
  • Engage with local businesses, partners and customers’ posts.
  • Track which posts drive saves, shares, profile visits and link clicks — not just likes.

Days 61–90: amplify and convert

  • Turn your best-performing organic posts into ads.
  • Retarget website visitors and video viewers with a clear offer.
  • Run one campaign per month tied to a specific product, service or promotion.
  • Review results and double down on the pillars and formats that convert.

What to measure

Reach and engagement tell you whether content resonates; website clicks, enquiries and sales tell you whether it pays. Review monthly and adjust the plan rather than abandoning it.

Conclusion

Social media works for small businesses when it’s focused, consistent and connected to an offer. Choose your platforms, commit to your pillars and calendar for 90 days, and let the data show you where to invest next.

Structured data and consistent business information help AI systems understand who you are.

faqs: What is AI SEO or GEO?
AI SEO (sometimes called generative engine optimisation or GEO) means optimising your content and brand so AI-powered search experiences can understand, trust and cite you.
Does schema markup help with AI Overviews?
Schema doesn’t guarantee inclusion, but it makes your facts — services, prices, FAQs, organisation details — unambiguous for search engines and AI systems that read your pages.
Do I need an llms.txt file?
It’s an emerging convention, not a ranking requirement. A short, accurate llms.txt summarising your business and key pages is low effort and can help AI tools that use it.
Will AI search reduce my website traffic?
Some simple informational queries get answered directly. But being cited builds trust and brand recall, and commercial queries still drive clicks to the sources that best answer them.
posts.content:
Customers increasingly ask AI — Google’s AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot — instead of scrolling through ten blue links. These systems summarise answers and cite a handful of sources. The businesses that get cited are the ones whose content is easiest to understand, verify and trust. Here’s how to become one of them.

How AI search chooses its sources

AI answers are built on top of search indexes and trusted data. In practice, the sources that get cited tend to:

  • Rank well already for the underlying query (SEO still matters).
  • State the answer clearly, near the top of the page.
  • Back claims with specifics: numbers, steps, comparisons, examples.
  • Come from a recognisable, consistent entity with real-world signals (reviews, mentions, profiles).

Step 1: write answer-first content

Open each page with a one- or two-sentence direct answer to the main question, then expand. Use question-led headings (“How much does SEO cost?”), short paragraphs, lists and tables. This is the same structure that wins featured snippets — and it makes your content easy to quote accurately.

Step 2: cover topics completely

AI systems favour sources that cover a topic thoroughly. Build clusters: a main service page supported by guides that answer related questions, all linked together. Our own SEO service page links to guides like how much SEO costs and our technical SEO audit checklist for exactly this reason.

Step 3: make your facts machine-readable

  • Structured data: Organization, LocalBusiness, Service, Product/Offer, FAQPage and Article schema.
  • Consistent business details: the same name, address, phone and description everywhere.
  • Clear pricing pages: real numbers in HTML text and tables, not only in images.
  • An llms.txt file: a short summary of who you are, what you offer and your key pages.

Step 4: strengthen your brand as an entity

AI recommendations lean heavily on what the wider web says about you. Keep your Google Business Profile complete and active, earn reviews on trusted platforms, get mentioned in relevant publications and directories, and make sure your social profiles link back to your site. Quality link building and digital PR help here too.

Step 5: show real expertise

Named authors with genuine experience, original insights and up-to-date information signal trust. Google’s guidance on helpful, reliable, people-first content applies just as much to AI search.

Step 6: keep the technical basics right

AI crawlers can only use what they can access. Don’t block reputable search and AI crawlers in robots.txt unless you have a reason to, keep pages fast and server-rendered where possible, and avoid hiding key information behind scripts or images.

How to track AI visibility

Regularly ask AI tools the questions your customers ask and note whether you’re cited. Watch Search Console for impressions on question-style queries, and track brand searches and referral traffic from AI tools in your analytics.

Conclusion

AI search doesn’t replace SEO — it raises the bar. Clear answers, complete topic coverage, machine-readable facts and a trusted brand are what get you cited. Start with your most important service pages and work outward.

  4. Product schema with price, availability and reviews.
  5. Helpful content — buying guides and comparisons that earn links.
  6. Clean technical setup: no duplicate URLs from filters and variants.

How to choose

  • Choose WooCommerce if content marketing is central to your growth, you need custom functionality, or you sell services and bookings alongside products.
  • Choose Shopify if you want to launch fast, sell physical products, and prefer a hosted platform with minimal maintenance.

Building a new store? Our E-Commerce Basic package sets up Shopify or WooCommerce with cart, checkout and payments from $799, and E-commerce SEO helps it rank. See website packages →

Conclusion

The platform matters less than how well the store is built and optimised. Pick the one that fits your team and growth plan, then invest in unique content, clean structure and speed — that’s what ranks and converts.
